# Results — Study 390 (Activist-13D)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The folklore that a stock
**pops and keeps drifting up** after an activist files a **Schedule 13D**, tested on a
**transparent, hardcoded basket of 25 famous activist campaigns** (Icahn, Elliott, Third
Point, Pershing Square, Trian, ValueAct, Starboard, …). For each campaign we pull the
target's and SPY's daily adjusted closes (yfinance, no key), measure the **announcement
pop** (day-0 return — the news being priced in) and the **post-announcement excess drift**
vs SPY if you buy **one day after** the announcement and hold 1 / 3 / 6 months. Run `python
examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted closes — 25 activist targets + SPY (public, no key) |
| Event set | **hardcoded** table of 25 well-known activist 13D campaigns, 2012–2024 announcements |
| Window | 2010-01-04 → 2026-06-18 (**4,140** trading days; **16.5** years of price tape) |
| Pop | day-0 return of the target (first trading day on/after the announcement) |
| Drift | target − SPY excess return; **1-day** entry lag; hold 1 / 3 / 6 months |
| Costs | one 10-bps round-trip on the buy-and-hold drift trade |

> **Selection caveat (named on the Signal axis).** A hardcoded basket of *famous*
> campaigns is **selected on outcome**: activist 13Ds enter folklore precisely because
> they were prominent and often profitable (Icahn/Apple, Elliott/Salesforce). That bias
> runs **in favour** of the claim — so a basket tilted toward memorable wins is the
> *easiest* possible test, and it still fails to clear significance. One target (TWTR,
> taken private in 2022) is absent from the free feed; 25 of 26 campaigns priced. The
> verdict does not hinge on the exact roster: a once-per-name event measured on ~25
> outcome-selected names is statistically underpowered, which holds *a fortiori* for a
> random, non-cherry-picked 13D sample.

## The announcement pop — real news, but you can't trade it

The day-0 return is the market re-pricing the filing. You cannot capture it unless you knew
the 13D was coming (you didn't), so it is **not a strategy** — it is the efficient-market
bump. We report it to show the news is real:

| | n | mean | median | win-rate | one-sample *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| announcement pop (day 0) | 24 | **+1.22%** | +0.62% | 62% | **+0.99** |

A ~1.2% average pop, positive more often than not — but even *this* uncapturable day-0 move
is only **t = 0.99** on this basket (several names had already run up before the filing was
public). The news matters; it is also small and already in the price.

## The signal — post-announcement excess drift vs SPY (the only tradable leg)

Buy at the close **one day after** the announcement (no look-ahead), hold H months, measure
the return **in excess of SPY** over the same window. The placebo *p* is the share of 20,000
random-date baskets — same horizon, **same targets** — whose mean excess matches/beats the
announcement basket (so it nulls out the targets' own drift, isolating the *timing*).

| horizon | n | mean excess | median excess | win-rate | Welch *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 1-month | 25 | **+1.74%** | +1.36% | 64% | **+1.11** | 0.183 |
| 3-month | 25 | **+0.89%** | +1.53% | 56% | **+0.40** | 0.449 |
| 6-month | 25 | **+3.78%** | +3.16% | 60% | **+0.98** | 0.283 |

Read it carefully. The drift is **positive at every horizon** — the folklore points the
right way. But it **never clears the t ≥ 2 bar** (the best is t = 1.11 at one month), the
placebo says a random-date basket on the *same names* beats it **~1 time in 4–5**
(p = 0.18–0.45), and it is non-monotone (it *shrinks* from 1m to 3m before recovering at
6m). A positive-but-insignificant, horizon-wobbly point estimate — measured on **25
outcome-selected events** — is not an edge.

## Costs barely matter — which is itself the point

| horizon | n trades | gross excess | net @ 10 bps round-trip |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 1-month | 25 | +1.74% | +1.64% |
| 3-month | 25 | +0.89% | +0.79% |
| 6-month | 25 | +3.78% | +3.68% |

A 10-bps round-trip shaves ~0.1pp off a multi-month hold — costs are **not** the problem.
The problem is **significance and frequency**: a famous-activist 13D you can act on is a
once-in-a-while event whose post-announcement excess is inside the noise. You cannot
allocate NAV to a signal that (a) is statistically indistinguishable from buying the same
names on random dates and (b) only fires when an Icahn-scale name shows up.

## Robustness — flat in the entry lag, and a few names carry it

| variant | n | mean excess (6m) | Welch *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| lag = 0 (same-day) | 25 | +3.88% | 1.09 | 0.277 |
| **lag = 1 (headline)** | 25 | +3.78% | 0.98 | 0.283 |
| lag = 2 | 25 | +5.33% | 1.13 | 0.195 |
| lag = 5 | 25 | +4.78% | 1.03 | 0.223 |
| **drop AAPL / MSFT / DIS (mega-caps)** | 22 | **+2.49%** | **0.60** | 0.370 |

Shifting the entry from same-day to a week later barely moves the *t* (it never approaches
2), so the result is not an execution artefact. But removing just the three mega-cap targets
**halves the mean and pushes *t* to 0.60** — the modest positive estimate is carried by a
handful of names, exactly the fragility you'd expect when the basket was selected on fame.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful, and small samples are weak

On a deterministic set of **25 synthetic 13D events** (each target a GBM path sharing a
market factor, an announcement pop on day 0, and a *known* post-announcement excess drift):

| planted 6-month drift | detected | mean excess | win-rate | Welch *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **0.00** (no drift) | 25 | +3.64% | 52% | 0.72 | 0.262 |
| **+0.20** (huge edge) | 25 | +27.80% | 80% | **4.45** | **0.000** |

With **no** planted drift the test does **not** cross t = 2 (it cannot manufacture
significance from ~25 events, even when noise tilts the point estimate to +3.6%). Only a
**huge** planted edge — +20% excess over six months — drives *t* to 4.5. The control proves
two things at once: the measurement engine is unbiased, **and** ~25 events is too few to
detect any drift of plausible magnitude. The real-tape *t* of ~1 is exactly what an *absent
or tiny* drift looks like through a 25-event keyhole.

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The folklore points the right way: the announcement pop (**+1.22%**)
  and the post-announcement drift (**+1.74% / +0.89% / +3.78%** at 1/3/6m) are all positive.
  But none clears the **t ≥ 2 bar** (best t = 1.11), the placebo says a random-date basket on
  the same names matches it ~1 in 4–5, and dropping three mega-caps collapses it (t = 0.60).
  Literature support + a positive-but-insignificant, fragile point estimate on an
  **outcome-selected** basket ⇒ **WEAK**, not REAL.
- **Tradability — FRAGILE.** Costs are negligible, but the tradable leg (buy one day after
  the filing) delivers an excess return **inside the noise**, carried by a few names, on a
  rare event. Not a NAV-scale strategy.
- **Free lunch? — BUSTED.** "Buy the 13D and ride the activist" is a **selection illusion**:
  remember the Icahn/Apple wins, forget the duds, and a basket of legends *looks* like a free
  ride. On the only leg you can actually trade — after the news is public — the average drift
  is statistically indistinguishable from buying the same names on random dates.
